data.title: Holiday Loss Prevention: Why Visible Security Is Critical In Peak Season
data.description:
Retailers invest significant time and resources into creating positive customer experiences. From store layouts and staffing to technology and service standards, every detail is designed to make shopping easier, more engaging, and more efficient. Yet one important component of that experience is often overlooked: security.

As retail environments become increasingly complex, security can no longer be viewed solely through the lens of theft prevention. It also supports store operations, protects employees, and creates an environment where shoppers feel comfortable.

The challenge for retailers isn’t simply determining how much security they need. It’s understanding how security can complement the shopping experience without disrupting it.

A Visible Presence Can Serve More Than One Purpose

Retail theft is often opportunistic. Busy aisles, distracted employees, and high customer traffic can create vulnerabilities, particularly during major sales events and seasonal shopping periods. A visible security presence can help discourage opportunistic theft by signaling that a location is being monitored. But visibility’s value goes beyond deterrence.

When positioned appropriately, security professionals can help maintain orderly entrances, monitor higher-risk areas, and deliver an additional layer of support when unexpected situations arise.

Placement matters. A large-format retailer with multiple entrances and high foot traffic may require a different approach than a luxury boutique with controlled access and personalized service.

Rather than applying a uniform security model across every location, retailers should evaluate their specific operating environments, customer expectations, and historical loss patterns. The objective is to create a presence that is noticeable when needed but never unnecessarily intrusive.

Security and Customer Experience Are Not Competing Priorities

Retailers sometimes approach security and customer experience as separate functions. In practice, the two are closely connected.

Consider a busy store during a major promotional event. Long checkout lines, crowded entrances, and frustrated customers can quickly create operational problems. Employees may already be stretched thin, making it difficult to manage disruptions while maintaining service standards. In these situations, professional security personnel can provide valuable support through situational awareness, clear communication, and an understanding of established store procedures.

Equally important is how security professionals engage with customers. An overly aggressive or restrictive approach can undermine the welcoming environment retailers work hard to create. Conversely, a calm, professional presence can support confidence without making customers feel uncomfortable or scrutinized.

Effective retail security requires understanding the brand environment as much as the potential threats within it.

De-escalation is a Business Imperative

One of the most important capabilities in customer-facing security is knowing how to respond when tensions increase. An incident involving suspected theft, an upset customer, or a disagreement at an entrance can escalate quickly if handled poorly. The consequences may extend well beyond the original disruption and could affect employee safety, customer relationships, business operations, and company reputation.

This is why de-escalation, sound judgment, and adherence to established procedures are essential. Security professionals must evaluate situations, communicate effectively, and know when to involve store management or emergency responders. The goal should be to reduce risk, not cause additional confrontation.

In an environment where incidents can be recorded and shared publicly almost instantly, a measured and professional response is not only a safety consideration. It is also an important part of protecting the retailer’s reputation.

A Layered Approach Supports More Effective Operations

Not every security concern requires a permanent officer stationed in one location. Retailers should consider how different security capabilities can work together to address vulnerabilities across their properties.

For example, uniformed officers may provide a visible presence in customer-facing areas, while mobile patrols can help monitor parking lots, loading zones, and exterior access points. Remote monitoring technologies can provide additional visibility across locations or areas that may not require continuous on-site coverage. The right combination depends on the environment, operating hours, historical incidents, and business priorities.

Retailers can also use available loss prevention data to identify recurring patterns and make more informed decisions about resource allocation. A location experiencing repeated incidents near high-value merchandise may benefit from adjusting officer positioning. Another location may face greater challenges after closing, when employees leave and exterior areas need additional attention.

By aligning security resources with actual operational necessities, retailers can build a more adaptable and effective approach to protection.

Planning for Security Should Extend Beyond the Holiday Season

Although the holidays often bring increased attention to retail loss prevention, changing security demands occur throughout the year. Back-to-school shopping, product launches, major promotions, and seasonal sales can all create temporary increases in consumer traffic and operational pressure.

Retailers may also need additional coverage during renovations, overnight maintenance, inventory projects, or other activities outside normal business hours. These situations reinforce the significance of proactive planning. Rather than waiting for a problem to emerge, retailers should evaluate upcoming operational changes, assess possible vulnerabilities, and set clear expectations with their security providers.

When temporary coverage is required, that planning should include defined responsibilities, site-specific instructions, communication protocols, and appropriate operational oversight.

Flexibility is important, but it must never come at the expense of preparedness or accountability.

Rethinking Security as Part of the Retail Experience

The retail industry keeps evolving, and security expectations are evolving with it.

Today’s security strategies must do more than confront potential losses. They have to account for the realities of customer-facing environments, employee safety, and the operational pressures retailers navigate every day. That requires a thoughtful balance of visible deterrence, professional judgment, technology, and preparation.

When security is integrated into broader retail operations, it becomes more than a protective measure. It becomes an important contributor to a safer, more consistent, and more positive shopping experience.

Ultimately, effective retail security isn’t simply about protecting what a business sells. It’s about protecting the environment in which business happens.

Monika Brown is Vice President of Operations at Securitas Security Services USA, Inc., with more than 17 years of leadership experience, including six years in the Middle East. With expertise in retail security operations, loss prevention, and scalable security solutions, she brings a practical perspective to evolving security challenges. Monika champions professional standards, workforce preparedness, and operational accountability, helping organizations balance risk mitigation with business continuity, customer experience, and the changing demands of modern security environments.
data.author: Monika Brown, Securitas Security Services USA, Vice President of Operations

data.title: For Small Business Saturday, 2026 Holiday Shoppers Plan to Spend Where the Value Is Clear
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • More than half of Americans plan to shop on Small Business Saturday in 2026, but consumers are prioritizing clear value, convenience and fast service as holiday budgets remain under pressure.
  • AI is becoming a bigger part of the holiday shopping journey, influencing gift discovery, price comparison and retailer selection even as most shoppers stop short of letting AI complete purchases for them.

More than half of Americans plan to shop on Small Business Saturday this year, according to the third annual AT&T Business Holiday Shopping Survey, a signal that local retail still has a seat at the table during the most competitive shopping stretch of the year.

The AT&T research, along with those from Salesforce, KPMG, Walmart and Southpaw Insights, makes clear that shoppers in 2026 are spending more carefully. Budgets are tighter, expectations are higher and AI is now part of how consumers find deals and choose where to buy.

Small Business Saturday, falling on Nov. 28 this year, interest remains strong, according to the third annual AT&T survey as 52% of Americans plan to shop: 34% in person and 24% online.

Local Appeal, Big-Retailer Expectations on SBS

Shoppers want what small businesses already offer, including personal service and community ties. But they also expect the speed and convenience of larger retailers. Seven in ten expect a same-day response to a message or inquiry, including 20% who expect a reply within an hour. Text (40%), email (39%) and phone calls (38%) are the channels shoppers find most helpful.

“Shoppers want the warmth of a neighborhood shop with the ease of a big retailer, and small businesses shouldn’t have to choose between them,” said Matt Cook, senior vice president of Mid-Markets Sales at AT&T Business, in a statement.

Consumer Confidence Is Unsteady Heading Into the Holiday Season

Small businesses face those expectations in a holiday season that’s hard to forecast. Nikki Baird, vice president of strategy and product at Aptos, said that early forecasts were bullish, but consumer confidence has slipped since then. Shoppers are carrying heavier debt loads, and much of the spending growth in recent years has come from upper-income households whose wealth is tied to the stock market.

“I feel like I say this every year, that it’s really uncertain,” Baird told ReatilTouchPoints.com. “But this year is uncertain in different ways than it’s been uncertain in the past.”

Online shopping with small businesses is gaining ground. AT&T Business found preference for shopping online with small businesses rose five percent from the year before to 37%, while preference for large retailers fell the same percentage points to 63%.

How shoppers find small businesses depends on their age. Gen Z shoppers are nearly twice as likely to discover small businesses through social media as through word of mouth (37% vs. 19%). Boomers are more than three times as likely to rely on word of mouth as social media (30% vs. 9%). That points to two different outreach strategies: social content for younger customers and memorable in-store experiences that get older customers talking.

Consumers Plan to Spend, but Value Comes First

Holiday budgets are rising. KPMG’s Consumer Pulse Holiday 2026 survey found average holiday shopping spend will increase 5% to $783 as 45% of consumers expect to spend more, while 26% expect to spend less.

Salesforce reports a similar trend online. U.S. online sales from Oct. 1 through Nov. 15 rose 5% year over year and 5.5% globally. The company predicts Cyber Week, which runs Nov. 24 through Nov. 30, will produce a record $357 billion in global online sales and $84 billion in the U.S., each up 6%.

Retailers are responding with discounts. Salesforce found November discount rates are up 8% in the U.S. and 5% globally. As a result, average selling prices for physical goods are down 1% in the U.S. and 2% globally. Basket sizes are up 3%. “We’re expecting a blockbuster Cyber Week despite economic headwinds,” said Caila Schwartz, head of Agentic Commerce Shopper Insights at Salesforce.

Shopping Starts Earlier, but Last-Minute Demand Remains

More shoppers are planning ahead. Walmart’s Holiday Trend Report found 28% of shoppers expect to start earlier than last year, mainly to avoid a last-minute scramble and spread out spending. About two-thirds of Walmart gift purchases are planned ahead of time.

The Arkansas-based retailer’s survey found 38% of shoppers expect to do most of their holiday buying between October and the first half of November. Another 20% expect to do most of it between Thanksgiving weekend and Cyber Monday.

That does not mean panning doesn’t eliminate late demand as 34% of Walmart respondents stated gift purchases still happen in the moment, and half of its shoppers were still buying a week before Christmas last year. And AT&T Business found 45% of Americans would choose a nearby small business for a last-minute gift, compared with 32% who would choose a nearby large retailer.

AI Moves Into the Mainstream Shopping Journey

AI appears in all four retail-focused reports as a research and comparison tool. Baird cautioned traffic from AI sources still accounts for less than 5% of retailer site visits. That number misses how often AI shapes gift ideas and points shoppers toward a store before they ever click through.

“AI influence is definitely much broader than just AI traffic,” Baird said. “Would you have gone to this retailer if AI hadn’t said, ‘Hey, you should think about XYZ gift for this niece you’ve seen three times in the last three years’?”

Salesforce, who reported nearly 70% of shoppers are waiting for Cyber Week to make big purchases, predicts AI and shopping agents will influence $75.8 billion, or 21%, of global Cyber Week sales, up from $67 billion in 2025. AI-driven traffic to retailer websites is up 104% year over year. Shoppers who arrive through AI referrals are twice as likely to convert as other ecommerce shoppers.

Walmart reported that 53% of its surveyed customers say AI makes everyday tasks easier, and 39% say it helps them make better decisions. KPMG found consumers plan to use AI to:

  • Compare prices across retailers: 37%
  • Find discounts or promotions: 33%
  • Compare product reviews: 33%
  • Research gift ideas: 29%

While Salesforce found 74% of consumers trust AI recommendations, 73% aren’t ready to give a personal agent their credit card details. AT&T Business found 59% of adults wouldn’t let an AI assistant research and buy gifts for them, while 21% would use it for research only and 20% would use it for both.

AI Is Shaping How Consumers Research Gifts and Compare Retailers

AI influences which brands shoppers find. According to Salesforce, one in three shoppers discover new brands through AI assistants, and 11% say they won’t buy a product if AI advises against it. Brands that run their own shopper agents report gains: shoppers who use them spend 8% more per order and buy 23% more items.

That shift could work in favor of independent retailers. Baird said small businesses have fewer legacy systems and processes to work through than large chains. She added that platforms such as Shopify are surfacing smaller sellers in AI recommendations, which exposes shoppers to retailers they wouldn’t have found before.

“We see smaller businesses adopting a lot faster because it’s easier due to their size,” Baird said. “They can do things that were outside of their reach before or were really expensive and now are cheap.”

Omnichannel Convenience Is a Baseline Expectation

Shoppers move between digital and physical channels, and they expect both to work. In-store shopping remains the top holiday destination. Salesforce found 71% of shoppers plan to shop in store, including 63% of Gen Z. One in three Gen Z shoppers plans to visit a store for an early-morning Black Friday promotion.

The trip often starts online. AT&T Business found that before visiting a small business, 53% of consumers check its location, 47% check hours, 41% read reviews and 30% check inventory. Shoppers expect tools that once set large retailers apart. According to AT&T Business:

  • 43% expect online ordering.
  • 40% expect buy online, pick up in store.
  • 38% expect digital payments.
  • 38% expect text or email order updates.

Social media importance as a sales channel continues to grow as Salesforce found 23% of ecommerce traffic comes from social media clicks, up 13% year over year, led by TikTok and Instagram. Orders from social referrals grew 27% across October and November, and more than one in four shoppers bought something inside a social app in the past three months.

Payment preferences remain traditional. KPMG found cash (83%) and credit cards (80%) are the top choices, with buy now, pay later use rising.

Shoppers Are Cutting Carefully, Not Cutting Everything

At the forefront of all of this is consumers balancing higher spending with financial stress. Southpaw Insights’ American STRAIN study found seven in ten have made a major financial sacrifice, such as delaying bills, cutting back on food or taking on extra work. More than a third (34%) fall into the study’s “Under Pressure” category, and 42% say one unexpected expense would put them in serious financial trouble.

Yet 82% say there’s at least one thing they would keep buying even if they had to cut back on basics. “A consumer can keep buying your product while quietly cutting something else,” said Jessica Broome, Ph.D., founder of Southpaw Insights.

KPMG found similar tradeoffs. Planned monthly spending is rising on groceries (27%), gas and maintenance (21%) and personal care (10%). It’s falling on toys (11% decline), gaming (10% decline), hobby supplies, furniture and office supplies. Walmart’s data adds detail on gifting. Gift cards are the most popular gift this year at 36%, ahead of toys and games at 35%. Meaning to the recipient matters to 53% of shoppers. And 32% say a good deal prompts them to treat themselves, led by fashion and apparel (25.2%) and food and holiday meals (24.8%).

Loyalty is conditional. KPMG found about one-third of consumers plan to stay with retailers they trust, but they may switch for a significantly better deal. Southpaw found 73% appreciate brands that help them save without making them feel judged, and 68% still care about quality when money is tight.

Small Businesses Benefit as Shoppers Seek Trust, Quality and Connection

That demand for trust and quality plays to small businesses’ strengths. Baird said a long-running consumer push to put the phone down and embrace nostalgic hobbies is gaining ground as technology spreads. She said that shift gives retailers a chance to make holiday shopping about real-life connection and making memories again.

“The more artificial things are, the more people seek genuineness and in person,” Baird said. “Those are the ways that they connect to that in-personness.”

For this Small Business Saturday, industry experts forecast consumers to spend for the 2026 holiday season as they will reward retailers that make value obvious and buying easy.
data.author: james.hickey

data.title: The Backbone Battle: The Right AI Architecture Will Win the Store
data.description:
Retailers are in danger of repeating the mistakes of several former technology integration waves that resulted in disconnected systems, siloed data, costly integrations, and inconsistent reporting. Only this time with AI.

Acting now matters, because within five years, retailers won’t compete on AI applications in isolation or on a single platform. They will compete on how effectively they connect multiple AI capabilities, data, systems and workflows and operationalize the intelligence generated across their retail business ecosystem.

The retailers who fail to establish an AI backbone as foundation for scaling intelligence across the business run the risk of falling behind.

The New Operational Layer of the Value-Driving Store Ecosystem

One thing is for sure: AI is becoming the operational layer of the retail enterprise – the way POS became the transaction layer a generation ago. The potential is huge: Higher productivity in every store that can be accomplished with the same resources by automating routine tasks and improving operational efficiency.

Store associates can spend less time in the checkout area or on manual processes and more time on customer service and value-add tasks. Revenue per square foot can be increased through better merchandising, product availability and customer experience, while better inventory efficiency ensures the right products are available at the right time. Margins improve with lower operating costs, reduced shrink or smarter pricing.

Last but not least, it strengthens long-term customer relationships through personalized and frictionless experiences that increase loyalty, repeat visits and spending over time.

To shape the unified commerce environments of tomorrow that strongly connect physical and retail operations, seamless integration of AI-powered applications and scalability are key. And this requires more than just collecting AI capabilities.

From Applications to Architecture

What we are hearing from retailers is that they are moving from AI curiosity to AI value. A year ago, many conversations focused on testing AI. Today, the discussion is increasingly about measurable business outcomes such as labor productivity, inventory optimization, shrink reduction, forecasting accuracy and customer experience.

The market is shifting from pilots to operational impact. Instead of simply alerting managers to growing checkout queues, retailers want systems that automatically recommend or initiate corrective actions. They want AI that predicts friction and helps prevent it instead of just identifying self-checkout interventions after they occur. They are looking for AI-driven processes that anticipate stock issues and trigger replenishment decisions, or intelligent workflows that surface the next best action in real time instead of relying on associates to interpret multiple dashboards.

But, AI adoption is still accelerating faster than the underlying infrastructure. We experienced that many retailers have accumulated isolated AI use cases that often rely on separate data sets, vendors and workflows. As a result, scaling AI across the enterprise is proving much harder than deploying the initial use case.

Start Small with AI Solutions

An AI platform that serves as the backbone for the entire store ecosystem can solve that and matters more than the applications themselves when considering productivity and margin impact. A unified commerce platform that centralizes business logic and databases enables scalable AI, enterprise-wide data sharing, and the flexibility to integrate new solutions from a rapidly evolving AI menu.

With such a singular platform in place, retailers can start small with one AI solution like item recognition at the checkout to speed up the scanning process for the shopper. As they evolve and wish to implement more solutions, having that backbone in place enables them to add solutions and share image and video databases, product information, business logic and more between the different AI applications.

To stick with this example, the item recognition can help to reduce theft by exchanging data with an AI-powered shrink solution, minimizing the risk of shoppers maliciously trying to scan high-value items labeled as cheaper produce at the self-service checkout. This flexibility provides retailers with the vehicle to scale long term and ultimately get to the store of the future, whatever that future vision is for them.

Build the Intelligent Store

Imagine this: A customer plans a dinner in a retailer’s app, browsing products without making a purchase. Behind the scenes, a unified commerce platform combines that activity with real-time inventory, loyalty data, local conditions, and demand forecasts.

When the shopper enters the store, the experience is already personalized: relevant products are highlighted, inventory is aligned with expected demand, and associates receive replenishment tasks based on emerging shopping patterns. The result is a seamless connection between digital intent and physical operations, creating a shopping journey that continues naturally across channels rather than starting over at the store entrance.

This is just an example showing that tomorrow’s retail environments will operate and interact differently, combining digital insights with data from hundreds of models and sensors including computer vision, IoT, RFID, and workforce systems. When operating as a single collaborative intelligence, thousands of micro-decisions an hour will be made with minimal human orchestration: rebalancing labor, adjusting pricing signals, triggering replenishment or rerouting traffic.

The question is: How to prepare for this?

A Simple Phased Approach Can Set the Foundation

Beginning with an evaluative step-by-step approach allows retailers to ultimately reach an Intelligent Store scenario where there are hundreds of AI solutions deployed across a physical and digital environment. Providing interconnectivity between those solutions is critical for the ability to scale and for ease of deployment.

Before setting their AI foundation in place, retailers should consider a simple phased approach:

  1. Start with a business outcome. Define the specific business goals to achieve, such as increasing throughput, enhance workforce productivity, reducing costs or enhancing customer loyalty.
  2. Build the AI backbone. Establish a connected data and technology foundation that enables AI-driven insights, automation and decision-making.
  3. Deploy high-value use cases. Implement proven applications that deliver measurable results quickly, such as inventory optimization, labor scheduling or loss prevention.
  4. Scale via ecosystem partners. Expand capabilities and accelerate innovation by integrating solutions and expertise from technology and industry partners.
  5. Optimize through shared intelligence. Continuously improve performance by leveraging data, insights, and learnings across stores, channels and business functions.

The Digital Backbone of the Store

AI can provide individual benefits and evolve in each store and across the organization to provide seemingly endless unified commerce benefits, but the complexities of deploying multiple AI solutions across an estate are enormous. When implementing any AI applications, it’s important to consider how you will scale these solutions from the start.

To scale, retailers should have an AI backbone that holds the underlying business logic and common elements. AI learning models sit on top as individual applications. In this scenario, the application utilizes the underlying business logic from the platform, but the applications are agnostic to it.

This also enables retailers to collect an ecosystem of AI partners all attached to the AI backbone, so they can scale and manage solutions without duplication and multiple APIs, integrations, and partners to manage.

All in all, one thing is hard to ignore: AI is becoming the nervous system of the store. The retailers that can scale and operationalize intelligence fastest will create the greatest competitive advantage. And the retailers that successfully build that foundation today will be the ones defining the Intelligent Store era.

As Vice President of Global Solutions & Consulting (Banking & Retail), Matt Redwood leads the solutions engine within Diebold Nixdorf’s CRO organization, orchestrating a global mandate spanning the US, EMEA, & APAC. His focus is on architecting the convergence of high compliance financial systems and high velocity retail environments to redefine the future of global commerce. In the past years, Matt was the main driver of establishing Diebold Nixdorf’s AI platform Vynamic Smart Vision that helps retailers to combat the main causes of shrink & friction in retail, featuring AI-powered solutions for shrink reduction, age estimation, item recognition and more at the self-checkout and beyond.
data.author: Matt Redwood, Diebold Nixdorf, Vice President, Global Solutions & Consulting Group-Banking & Retail

data.title: AnswerLab: AI Use Rising Despite Costing Users
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • AnswerLab found consumers want AI to research, compare and draft but not make final decisions for them.
  • Roughly 80% of participants check AI’s work, and more than 20% of Commerce participants called customer service chatbots frustrating, circular or “a dead end.”

A new report from AnswerLab finds a growing gap between what AI products assume people want and what people actually do— with some of the most notable evidence coming from those who can describe how AI is wearing down their effort and confidence as they keep using it anyway.

The Assumption Gap: How People Are Setting Their Own Rules for AI draws on three years of insight from hundreds of research engagements, a review of public research, and conversations with experts in patient advocacy, vehicle safety, machine learning, and digital trust. The AI-moderated interviews with 334 people— including two cohorts of teens— described how they use AI, where they stop, and what they do when products don’t support the distinctions they need.

Across every domain, from grocery shopping to healthcare to the classroom, participants wanted AI to research, compare, and draft, but not decide. For instance, identical language across categories included: “I want to approve it myself.” and “That’s where I draw the line.” The most experienced users were most likely to build their own rules, down to exact dollar thresholds and category exclusions.

Why Are Consumers Setting Their Own Rules for AI?

Megan Malli, CEO at AnswerLab stated consumers are already setting the rules for how AI fits into their lives, purchase by purchase, message by message, action by action, without any company asking them to.

“People aren’t waiting for anyone to hand it to them and, frankly, are showing us that they’ll use AI, but on their own terms, in a way they’re comfortable with after building that sense of trust,” said Malli in a statement. “The companies that build for that instinct, instead of trying to design around it, are the ones that will earn trust fastest.”

How Does AI Affect User Confidence and Workload?

Heavy AI users, teens in particular, can describe exactly how AI is changing their thinking, and they still can’t stop using it.  The difference came down to how people used the tool. Across the study, participants who used AI to understand a topic, test results, a lease, or a homework concept described feeling more prepared and more willing to push back. Those who used it to skip the work described dependency. The same technology built confidence when it explained and wore it down when it did the work.

Introducing AI into workflows was intended to automate tasks, but across the study, people described managing AI as an unaccounted-for second job: briefing AI, coordinating it across tools, checking its output, and keeping it running. Roughly 80% of participants across five study domains described a habit of checking AI’s work. In Health and School, where the question was asked directly, the number was highest. In Work, Commerce, and Home, participants volunteered the behavior unprompted.

In the Home study, coordination was the most widely shared complaint. One participant counted roughly ten apps running their house. Another builds routines across devices by hand because “none of those apps are really trying to make things easier for me.” The promise is a home that runs itself in the background, but the reality is a stack of separate tools connected by the person who lives there.

How Do Consumers Use AI Before They Reach a Retailer?

By the time customers arrive at a business, many have already had something close to a consultation with their own AI, and the company’s front door may never open. Roughly 70% of Commerce participants found AI review summaries useful for making purchase decisions faster. Nearly half described using AI to plan travel by compiling itineraries, amenities, and prices across a variety of online sources.

Participants want AI to do more of the homework: hunt prices across retailers, verify sellers, and track loyalty rewards. But ultimately, they want to continue making the decisions themselves. More than 20% of Commerce participants – unprompted – described customer service chatbots as frustrating, circular, or “a dead end.” What bothered them was less what the bots couldn’t do than the fact that the bots’ answers served the company’s interests over the consumers’.

Click here to download the full AnswerLab Signature Report.

data.title: Intelligent Connections Are the Key to the AI-enabled Path to Purchase
data.description:
The path to purchase begins long before a shopper enters a store or even visits a retailer’s website. It now stretches across a growing ecosystem of digital touchpoints where consumers use AI-powered tools to research products, compare prices, evaluate alternatives and confirm availability. By the time shoppers walk through the door, many already know what they want, what it costs and whether it is in stock.

However, the challenge for retailers extends beyond deploying new applications at individual touchpoints. They must connect customer intelligence, inventory systems, store operations and the technology infrastructure. If these capabilities operate as standalone solutions, AI’s ability to improve the experience across the entire path to purchase will remain limited.

Realizing AI’s full potential requires an intelligent, connected foundation that spans associate devices, in-store systems, edge computing resources and cloud platforms. When data and intelligence move seamlessly across that ecosystem, each interaction informs and improves the next. As a result, retailers must think beyond individual applications to building an ecosystem that turns AI investments into measurable improvements in customer experience, operational efficiency and business performance.

Addressing the Gaps Between Channels

Dramatically increased visibility is one of the most important capabilities AI has brought to retail and the customer journey. Shoppers can determine what products are available and where long before they ever set foot in a store. Within the store, associates gain a more accurate understanding of inventory—what they have in stock, how much is available and where it is located.

However, the real test comes when something goes wrong.

Consider a shopper who discovers that the store location they just entered does not have the product they want. Any associate at that store should be able to identify the item elsewhere in its enterprise and immediately offer options: recommend another store that has it, offer to have it delivered or arrange another fulfillment method.

Despite this being a basic omnichannel promise, retailers often struggle to deliver it seamlessly because their current setups have these capabilities siloed. The technology only becomes truly omnichannel when the underlying systems can share information and act on it.

Why Pilots Struggle to Scale

While the customer experience is the visible result, infrastructure remains the challenge underneath it.

Oftentimes, retailers successfully pilot an AI implementation in one or two locations only to discover that scaling the same application across hundreds or thousands of stores is a fundamentally different—and more challenging—task. The existing technology at stores is simply insufficient for many of today’s AI-driven workloads.

For example, a conventional PC acting as a store server may not be sufficient for an environment running computer vision, processing massive volumes of sensor data and supporting multiple AI applications. Retailers must determine where to place each workload: what should run locally, what belongs at the edge and what should move to the cloud. They also must consider application management across distributed locations, data growth, new application integration through APIs, and security and isolation of workloads.

Considering the myriad factors, there is no one-size-fits-all answer for retailers, as the right architecture depends on the problems each one is trying to solve. However, those who approach AI from an infrastructure perspective are getting further, faster because they are starting the process by thinking and building beyond that initial proof of concept.

Infrastructure is the Foundation; Experience is the Metric

Shoppers do not care about the architecture or the creative use of AI behind an application. They simply want a seamless experience in which they know whether their desired product is available, whether an associate can answer their question, and whether they can complete their purchase without friction.

That is where connected AI becomes crucial.

An associate equipped with the right AI-backed tools could inquire about a product and receive an answer, product options and inventory information in one place. Considering the alternative is finding a colleague who may or may not have the answer or—worse—sending the customer to find them, this information at an associate’s fingertips is a massive capability that removes friction from the purchasing process.

Similarly, AI can help store teams manage daily operations by identifying changing traffic patterns, helping determine when another checkout lane should open or anticipating merchandising needs. If changing conditions create demand for a certain product the system can surface that information proactively before employees would otherwise react to it.

Agentic AI extends this concept further. Instead of simply identifying a situation, an agentic system can potentially connect that intelligence to an appropriate action without direct human intervention. However, the goal cannot be autonomy for autonomy’s sake. It must tie to a measurable outcome—less interruption, faster service and better decisions for employees and customers.

Autonomy Requires a Stronger Foundation

Furthermore, as retailers increase AI’s responsibility, foundational elements such as data quality and governance become even more important. Retailers need reliable datasets, clear guidelines and established guardrails before they can automate more complex tasks. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and other approaches can help ground outputs and reduce hallucinations, while agents designed and tested for defined tasks can provide a controlled starting point.

But the most important consideration remains the desired outcome.

If retailers are unclear about what they want to get from their AI investments, they will not know what to build. Beginning with a business problem—whether inventory accuracy, loss prevention, associate productivity, traffic analysis or another measurable objective—is critical.

Building the Foundation— Not Another Silo

Retailers planning significant AI investments must begin with three priorities: defining the business problem, designing compute and data architectures to address them and plan beyond the initial use case. Considering these together from the outset can prevent successful pilots from becoming isolated silos, creating a foundation capable of supporting both today’s priorities and tomorrow’s opportunities.

The retail organizations positioned to lead into 2027 will not necessarily be those deploying the greatest number of AI applications. They will be the ones building connected ecosystems capable of uniting data, intelligence and action across stores, edge environments and cloud platforms. Whether the objective is improving inventory accuracy, increasing associate productivity, reducing loss or enhancing customer engagement, AI investments must ultimately connect to measurable business outcomes.

The future of retail AI will be defined less by individual applications and more by how effectively they work together. By establishing a connected foundation, retailers can move beyond experimentation toward continuous innovation, empowering employees with better insights, delivering the seamless experiences customers increasingly expect and simplifying the path to purchase.

Pradeep Kumar is Global Vice President of Sales, leading Lenovo’s Vertical Industries Business. He works with retailers worldwide to transform store operations through AI and end-to-end technology solutions that drive business outcomes. His focus is helping retailers adopt AI and automation to make smarter decisions and create more personalized shopping experiences, and adapt quickly to market needs.

data.title: This Black Friday and Cyber Monday, the Shopper Might Be an AI Agent. Is Your Checkout Ready?
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • AI agents are starting to influence holiday shopping behavior, which means retailers need product data, site performance and checkout flows built for both humans and machine-led activity.
  • Checkout failures, stale content and weak monitoring can turn AI-driven discovery into lost sales during peak Black Friday and Cyber Monday traffic.

Black Friday and Cyber Monday have always tested whether retail websites can handle a surge of shoppers. In 2026, some of those shoppers may not be people.

AI is changing both sides of holiday shopping. Consumers use AI tools to find deals, compare products and decide what to buy. Retailers use AI for discovery, recommendations, pricing, fulfillment and post-purchase engagement. During the this years sales window, retailers need to serve human shoppers, AI crawlers, AI shopping assistants and agent-driven checkouts at the same time.

But this year, the question isn’t whether AI matters in retail, its whether their e-commerce infrastructure, product data and checkout systems are ready for it.

The New Holiday Shopper May Not Be Human

An estimated 182.7 million consumers plan to shop during the Thanksgiving weekend this year, according to the annual survey released yesterday by the National Retail Federation and conducted by Prosper Insights & Analytics. While down slightly from 186.9 million shoppers last year, the figure continues the trend of elevated shopping during the holiday weekend seen in recent years. Black Friday remains the most popular day to shop during Thanksgiving weekend, with 69% (126 million) planning to do so, followed by Cyber Monday at 36% (66.1 million). The 2026 holiday season is expected to be the first in which AI agents meaningfully shape how consumers discover, compare and possibly buy products. A report from Kinsta, a managed WordPress hosting provider, shows how far that shift has gone:

  • 59% of consumers use AI tools often or occasionally for research.
  • 53% sometimes or often skip company websites entirely during early research.
  • 61% believe AI will eventually replace traditional websites as the main way people discover products.

For retailers, that changes the peak-season question. It’s no longer only whether a website can handle more shoppers; can the site can handle more machine-led shopping activity without breaking the customer experience?

Discovery Is Changing Before Checkout Breaks

The AI shift starts well before payment. AI assistants now narrow options, compare products and make recommendations before a shopper reaches a retailer’s site.

That doesn’t mean consumers trust those recommendations blindly. According to Kinsta, 58% of consumers trust content less when they believe it was AI-generated. Only 18.8% trust AI product recommendations without doing their own research. And 44.7% always or most of the time visit a company’s website after receiving an AI recommendation.

“People are using AI to narrow their options, then coming to websites to make sure the recommendation checks out,” said Matt Reid, chief marketing officer at Kinsta. “Websites aren’t becoming less important because of AI. If anything they’ve become the crucial last line of defense against bad information.”

Checkout Is Where the Risk Becomes Measurable

Checkout is where AI shopping risk turns into lost orders and lost revenue. An AI agent may choose products, compare shipping costs, weigh total price and move toward purchase differently than a human. Checkout systems built around normal shopper behavior may not hold up under agent-led activity. Potential failures include:

  • Wrong items added to the cart
  • Budgets blown by shipping costs revealed late
  • Duplicate orders
  • Verification loops that stall the purchase
  • Payment or purchase-path failures

These aren’t abstract risks. In Marker.io’s survey of more than 90 practitioners, 37% raised broken links, buttons and forms as a recurring problem, a category that includes blocked checkout steps. Fritz Colcol, CMO of Iridium Clothing Co., noted  “the most dangerous bug on an ecommerce site is the one that looks correct.”

Timing is another problem. Many retail teams test the purchase flow at the end. By the time an agent reaches checkout, it may already have made key decisions based on product data, pricing and shipping information gathered earlier in the journey.

Retail Infrastructure May Be Underprepared

Retail teams find site problems after the damage is done. Marker.io asked e-commerce professionals how they first noticed a website mistake that nobody caught right away. For 36%, the first sign was the loss itself: a lost customer, falling sales or orders that stopped. Another 36% found the problem through a one-off audit or luck. Only 28% caught it through a routine check, and only routine checks caught mistakes before they cost money.

The report points to gaps in how sites are managed:

  • 63% of respondents named wrong or outdated content as the top problem, including old offers, mismatched prices and AI-generated errors.
  • 71% said pages go stale or fixes get undone after launch.
  • 40% said nobody clearly owns the site, the page or the fix.
  • 13% have automated checks watching the live site.

Traffic adds more pressure. AI crawlers can hit dynamic and uncached pages more often than human shoppers do, putting extra load on origin servers during the busiest days of the year. That makes Black Friday failure a revenue and retention problem, not just a technical one. Kinsta found that 61% of consumers associate website quality with the quality of a company’s products or services. A slow or broken site doesn’t just lose a sale. It can lose the customer.

What ‘Agent-Ready’ Should Mean

Retailers preparing for the holiday window can start with five checks:

Bot access: Make sure security tools aren’t blocking legitimate AI shopping agents along with malicious bots.

Product accuracy: Verify prices, titles, availability, shipping and promo logic across live and cached pages and product feeds.

Traffic capacity: Test site performance under human traffic and automated traffic at the same time.

Checkout reliability: Audit the full purchase flow for failures, loops, duplicate orders, tax and shipping errors, and wallet or payment issues.

Real-time monitoring: Watch live traffic, blocked requests, slowdowns, cart failures and checkout errors during peak sales windows.

Each check needs a named owner as with everyone able to publish to a site but nobody owning the final review, errors stay live.

AI May Reshape Who Wins the Holiday Season

AI could change which retailers capture holiday demand as brand familiarity may matter less than machine-readable product data, reliable fulfillment and a trustworthy site. But getting recommended is only step one. A recommendation doesn’t guarantee a sale if the product is out of stock, shipping costs surprise the buyer or checkout fails. Fulfillment becomes the deciding factor.

The post-purchase experience matters as well. AI-referred shoppers may be first-time buyers with no loyalty to the brand. Retailers that want those shoppers back will need accurate order updates, on-time delivery and easy returns.

Black Friday and Cyber Monday have always been a stress test for e-commerce. This year, the test has a new variable with AI shoppers. Retailers aren’t preparing only for more shoppers, they are preparing for more software acting like shoppers. The retailers that come out ahead will be the ones whose product data, checkout systems and monitoring work for both.

data.title: Holiday Shoppers Lean on Grocery Loyalty Programs to Save In 2026
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Shoppers would rather cut back on holiday clothing, décor or events than scale back their holiday meal, and 36% want loyalty member discounts to make Thanksgiving prep easier.
  • While 72% of shoppers say their store’s loyalty program is essential to saving, only 58% of shoppers earning under $35,000 are members, compared with 78% of those earning $150,000 or more.

As families prepare for the holidays this season, the centerpiece of the season remains the family holiday meal. And food shoppers are taking steps protect it in the current challenging economic environment, according to The Food Industry Association (FMI).

The U.S. Grocery Shopper Trends 2026: Holidays report from FMI found 45% of shoppers are extremely or very concerned about rising prices for holiday foods, up eight percentage points from a year earlier. Yet shoppers say they would rather cut back on holiday clothing, décor or events than scale back their holiday feast, turning to their grocery store’s loyalty program to make the math work.

When asked how grocers can make Thanksgiving prep easier, the top request is holiday discounts for loyalty program members (36%), followed by special displays for the holiday meal (29%) and for specific dishes (25%).

How Confident Are Shoppers About Their Grocery Budgets This Holiday Season?

The FMI’s U.S. Grocery Shopper Sentiment Index stands at 72 this fall, near its historical high.

“Food is what holds the holidays together, and shoppers are telling us they will protect the holiday meal even if it means trimming elsewhere,” said Leslie G. Sarasin, president and CEO, FMI , in a statement. “Concern about grocery prices remains high, but it has eased slightly since August, and the share of shoppers who feel in control of their grocery spending has climbed 13 points over the same period. In fact, for the first time since we began tracking holiday trends in August 2024, shoppers feel more in control of their grocery budgets than of their other major household expenses.”

How Are AI and Scratch Cooking Shaping Thanksgiving Meals in 2026?

The Thanksgiving and holiday dinners are being joined by AI in the kitchen this year. Weekly AI use among shoppers rose to 27% from 19% a year ago, and 65% would like to use AI to help plan holiday meals, most often to find new recipes (34%) or festive ideas (27%).

Among shoppers planning a turkey, 59% will make it from scratch at home, up 16 points from 2025, while freshly prepared turkey fell 10 points to 19%. Turkey (68%), mashed potatoes (63%), stuffing (62%) and a warm vegetable side (50%) all rose versus last year. Where at least one Thanksgiving dish is homemade, 95% of shoppers plan to help prepare the meal, and nearly as many are excited about the prep (90%) as the holiday itself (89%).

As they shopped for their Thanksgiving day meal, 24% are extremely or very concerned about holiday food out-of-stocks. But half said they would simply make a different familiar dish and 35% would try a new recipe.

Why Are Grocery Loyalty Programs Essential for Holiday Savings?

The report shows grocery loyalty programs are one of the most practical tools shoppers have for saving money this season. Of shoppers surveyed, 72% strongly or somewhat agree that their primary store’s loyalty program is essential to helping them save on groceries and stay within their budgets. Key attraction for loyalty programs include:

  • Members find real value, mostly through savings. When a program is offered, 71% of shoppers join, and 95% of members find their program at least somewhat valuable. Shoppers value the money-saving benefits most— general everyday savings and discounts (95%), personalized savings and discounts (91%), points to use on a variety of items (90%) and gas savings or points (86%).
  • Loyalty members enjoy shopping more. Shoppers who see their loyalty program as essential rate their primary store higher (85% vs. 79%) and are more likely to love or like grocery shopping (50% vs. 37%).
  • Demand outpaces access, and those who could save the most are missing out. Among shoppers whose primary store doesn’t offer a loyalty program, 68% are extremely or very interested in having one. Where programs exist, only 58% of shoppers earning under $35,000 are members, compared with 78% of those earning $150,000 or more.

“Loyalty programs are delivering exactly what shoppers need right now: everyday savings that help them stay on budget without giving up the holiday meals they love,” Sarasin said. “The opportunity ahead is making sure all shoppers, especially those in lower-income households and younger consumers, know these savings are available and find them easy to use.”

The full U.S. Grocery Shopper Trends 2026: Holidays report can be downloaded by clicking here.

data.title: The Last Mile Starts in the Warehouse: Why Fulfillment Visibility Is the Key to Omnichannel Success
data.description:
On the surface, last-mile delivery issues look like shipping problems. An order arrives late, a retailer flags a compliance violation or the wrong product arrives. The first instinct is to look at the carrier, but the root cause often lies within the fulfillment warehouse, where inventory, order management, processes and technology converge.

For omnichannel brands, this distinction matters. A delayed shipment can disappoint a customer, but a retail order that misses routing requirements or arrives with incorrect labeling can trigger chargebacks, jeopardize retailer relationships and put future business at risk. As a brand grows, the margin for operational errors shrinks.

The way to solve this is with greater visibility into fulfillment operations. With it, teams can determine whether an order is ready to ship correctly in the first place. A brand’s fulfillment provider should provide that visibility.

Why Fulfillment Is Overlooked in the Last Mile

Fulfillment is often treated as the step between receiving products and handing an order to a carrier. In reality, it’s one of the most complex stages of the supply chain.

To ensure an order arrives to the customer on time and as promised, it’s critical that inventory is recorded accurately, available quantities synchronized across sales channels, and orders picked, packed and labeled according to the specific retailer’s requirements. Each step depends on the accuracy of the one before it. A receiving discrepancy can lead to an inaccurate inventory count, while a picking or labeling error can turn an otherwise complete order into a costly compliance issue.

The warehouse or distribution center is the last opportunity to detect and correct these errors before a shipment enters the transportation network. After that, correcting a mistake becomes more difficult and expensive. For retail orders, the consequences can extend beyond an individual shipment compliance penalty and become a strained business relationship. Fulfillment is a crucial control point for protecting both the customer experience and the retail economics of an omnichannel business.

Visibility Is the Solution

Delivery issues can often be addressed earlier with better visibility into fulfillment operations. Too many brands still rely on tracking numbers or spreadsheets to confirm that an order has shipped. While these tools provide a snapshot of activity, they may not explain where a problem is occurring.

Meaningful operational visibility goes further. Brands need timely access to inventory levels, inbound receiving, open orders and shipment status, along with the ability to identify discrepancies without requesting a report or waiting for a warehouse contact to respond.

Teams having access to the same operational information enables small discrepancies to be addressed before they become a major disruption. It’s important that brands investigate an inventory mismatch before it affects a customer order. Likewise, a delayed inbound shipment can be identified before it creates a stockout.

Today’s modern and complex supply chain requires connected systems to provide data across the brand, its fulfillment partner and its sales channels, reducing the blind spots that emerge when each function operates independently. Visibility won’t eliminate every exception, but it can help teams detect, understand and resolve issues sooner.

Direct EDI: Connecting Retail Orders to Execution

Retail fulfillment adds a layer of complexity. Retailers have specific requirements for purchase orders, routing, shipping windows, labels and advance shipment notifications.

Electronic data interchange (EDI) enables businesses to exchange standardized documents electronically, translating retailer requirements into information that trading partners’ systems can process. But having EDI capability alone isn’t enough. The integration quality and ongoing management are equally important.

Disconnected systems, manual intervention and delayed messages can leave orders or exceptions unnoticed until a shipment misses its window. Direct EDI integration can reduce intermediary handoffs, while a well-managed EDI service helps ensure that document mapping, testing, monitoring and exception resolution are handled consistently.

The goal isn’t simply to connect systems. It’s also to ensure that retailer requirements reach the fulfillment operation accurately and that order and shipment information flows back to the relevant systems promptly. Integrating EDI with warehouse processes gives teams more time to address problems before they become chargebacks, missed delivery windows or rejected shipments.

Make Retail Compliance Part of the Workflow

One common mistake is treating retail compliance as a final checklist rather than an operational discipline. By the time a shipment reaches the loading dock, many important decisions have already been made. It’s important to build retail requirements into fulfillment workflows, with the right routing guidance, labeling, documentation and verification steps in place before orders leave the facility.

The same principle applies to inventory accuracy. Brands need reliable information about what is physically present, what is available to promise and what has already been committed. Without that foundation, even sophisticated order-routing technology can make poor decisions.

Choosing a third-party logistics (3PL) partner, therefore requires more than comparing shipping rates or warehouse capacity. Brands should understand how a prospective partner manages retail integrations, monitors exceptions, verifies orders and provides access to operational data. A capable partner helps identify risks and resolve issues proactively, rather than simply reporting what went wrong after a shipment leaves the building.

Takeaway: Fix the Process Before the Package Ships

Last-mile performance is shaped long before a carrier collects a package. Accurate inventory, connected systems, disciplined warehouse execution and timely information all influence whether an order reaches its destination correctly and on time.

As omnichannel brands grow, complexity can quickly rise. New retailers introduce new requirements, while higher order volumes can overwhelm manual workarounds that once seemed manageable. Without repeatable processes and reliable information, small problems can multiply into expensive bottlenecks.

Brands should evaluate whether their systems provide timely visibility across channels, whether retail requirements are built into fulfillment workflows and whether exceptions can be identified and resolved quickly.

Fulfillment visibility should be treated as a foundational capability, not just a reporting feature. Direct EDI integration, well-designed warehouse workflows and accessible operational data give teams more opportunities to catch discrepancies early and protect retail compliance.

No technology can prevent every mistake, and no integration replaces sound operational processes. But when information moves reliably between systems, teams can intervene before problems become expensive. The most effective last-mile strategy may begin by looking upstream.

With over 20 years of finance, sales, operations, and leadership experience, Dave Tu has led DCL during a transformational time of growth, taking the company from a regional logistics operator to a national domestic provider. He leads with a tech-forward mindset, often investing in new operational tech (robotics, automation, green energy) to give DCL’s customers the best possible market advantage in the ever-shifting ecommerce landscape.

data.title: 5 Ways Small Businesses Can Make Holiday Packages More Memorable
data.description:
Consider a customer who discovers your business online while holiday shopping. They may spend twenty minutes comparing some products, reading about your story, and placing their first order. A few days later, a plain brown box arrives on their porch containing the product and a packing slip. The product itself is excellent, but the experience of receiving it is indistinguishable from every other package delivered that week.

Small businesses can benefit from giving special attention to packaging, particularly during the fourth quarter. Holiday shoppers are often first-time buyers, prompted by a recommendation, a gift guide, or a search result. The package is the first physical object that business places in the customer’s hands, and it arrives at the only point in the transaction where a brand has the customer’s full attention and final evaluation.. Making your package memorable provides an unspoken advantage.

Most small businesses treat packaging as a line item in shipping costs, but approached deliberately, it functions as a marketing channel the customer has already agreed to receive. Here is where and why that investment pays off.

Begin with the Exterior

The outside of the box does the most work, which makes it one of the easiest ways for a small business to showcase their brand this season. It is what the customer sees on the doorstep, what sits on the kitchen counter while they find scissors, and what appears in the background if they photograph the contents.

Improving it does not require a massive (or expensive) overhaul. A branded sticker sealing a plain mailer accomplishes most of what a printed box does at a fraction of the cost. Custom packing tape delivers similar consistency on every order without requiring a significant volume commitment. For businesses that do invest in printed mailers, the more practical approach is to order one or two sizes used most often rather than a full range that will sit in storage until spring.

Treat the Interior as Part of the Product

Opening a box to find a product loose among packing peanuts communicates to a customer that presentation doesn’t matter, their order was one of many hastily packed and shipped. On the other hand, opening a package to find the product gift-wrapped in tissue paper and sealed with a sticker shows thoughtfulness and taste, and the cost difference is measured in cents per order.

Tissue paper, crinkle fill in a brand color, or a simple wrap-and-seal treatment introduces a brief pause between opening the box and reaching the product. That pause is the entire mechanism at work. It signals that someone considered and hand-wrapped this particular order, which remains one of the clearest distinctions and advantages between a small business and a fulfillment warehouse.

Add a Personal Signature Where it Counts

The most effective insert available to most small businesses costs nothing but time: a brief handwritten note.

It does not need to be long, and it should not be a form letter reproduced by hand. One or two lines referencing the specific order, the color selected, the likelihood that it is a gift, or the hope that it arrives on schedule or that the customer likes it, contributes more to customer retention than a comparable spend on acquisition.

Holiday volume can make this difficult to sustain across every order, and that constraint is worth planning around rather than abandoning the practice altogether. Reserving handwritten notes for first-time customers or for orders above a set value preserves most of the effect at a manageable workload. Where handwriting is genuinely impractical, printed note cards carrying a signature and a single handwritten line perform nearly just as well.

Give Every Package a Second Purpose

Each box shipped represents a delivery vehicle already paid for. Most businesses will send it out carrying nothing beyond the product itself.

A little something extra changes that calculation. Including a discount code redeemable in January is the familiar version, and it works precisely because it reaches the customer at the moment they are most favorably disposed toward the business. Other options are worth considering as well: a referral card the recipient can pass along, care instructions that reduce return rates, a percent off their next order, a QR code linking to a gift guide or exchange form, or a brief card explaining the business’s mission and values.

That final example carries more weight than it initially appears to. During the holidays, a substantial share of the people opening a business’s packages are not its customers. They are people its customers care about. Introducing the brand to that audience costs one printed card and reaches them at a moment of genuine goodwill.

Design the Set, Not the Pieces

The four tactics above are worth considerably more in combination than in isolation, and only when they share a cohesive visual language.

The discipline here mirrors what applies to storefront signage and direct mail: one color palette, one typeface pairing, one simple motif, applied consistently across every element. The sticker, the tissue paper, the note card, and the insert should read as a coordinated set. When they do, a customer ordering again in March recognizes the package before reading the label. When they do not, the packaging reads as an assortment of unrelated promotional purchases, which leaves a weaker impression than a plain box would have.

Achieving this does not require a design budget or outside help. It requires selecting a palette and a motif once, documenting them, and holding to those choices when the next order goes in during the November rush.

Measure Packaging Against the Next Order

There is a natural tendency to evaluate packaging against the transaction it accompanies, where it registers as pure expense. The return does not appear on that line. It appears in January, when a customer who received something that left an impression returns to the site directly instead of browsing competitors’ offerings.

Holiday volume represents the single moment in the year when a small business introduces itself to a large number of people simultaneously, most of whom may never encounter its advertising. What arrives on their doorstep is that introduction. A few dollars and some advance planning determine resonance and repeat purchases.

data.title: AI Plans Outrun Store Realities as Bad Stock Data Cost Retailers Millions
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Store associates say stock data matches the shelf just 46% of the time, and a retailer with 10,000 associates faces more than $41 million a year in labor costs to compensate.
  • Associates who took part in technology pilots used most store tools at a 74% rate and were twice as likely to report high trust in stock data as associates who were never asked for input.

Global research from Scandit reveals retail’s race to deploy AI is running ahead of the data reality inside its stores as associates reported that stock information matches what they find on the shelf just 46% of the time while only 8% trust store data completely.

This creates a costly gap between what the system says, what is actually in the store and what customers experience, while leaving AI and other technology investments to act on incomplete records. That gap is already being absorbed by labor as associates estimate they would each get back more than 4.4 hours a week, nearly six working weeks a year, if they had data they could trust.

A retailer employing 10,000 store associates, for example, faces more than $41 million a year in labor cost tied to compensating for the gap.

Is Retail’s AI Problem Really a Store Data Problem?

Retailers do not have an AI adoption problem as much as a store truth problem,” said Samuel Mueller, CEO and co-founder of Scandit.

“Associates are spending valuable time repairing these gaps, yet much of that work disappears into unofficial tracking systems,” said Mueller in a statement. “Before retailers ask AI to make more decisions based on inaccurate store data, they need a shared, accurate view of what is actually happening on the shelf and across their stores.”

What Is a “Shadow Store” in Retail?

The result is a ‘shadow store’ in which vital information exists outside the record that head office, dashboards and AI systems rely on. When the system is wrong, associates do what they have to do to keep the store running. Nearly half (49%) correct the record themselves and 44% raise a stock adjustment. But among associates who take action, 42% bypass the official system entirely, while 68% use at least one informal method, including paper notes, team chats, personal phone photos and apps or memory.

Associates’ trust in stock data does not build gradually. The survey highlights it stays low until the data is very good as only 8% of associates completely trust their store’s stock information, and only one in four say it is accurate more than 70% of the time.

Among associates who put accuracy anywhere up to 50%, roughly a quarter report high trust, and that figure barely moves until accuracy passes 70%, when it rises sharply.

How Does Inaccurate Stock Data Affect Customers and Technology Adoption?

The consequences extend beyond productivity. Associates report spending an average of 4.1 hours each week handling customer questions that store technology should be able to answer, and are asked to physically check whether an item is in stock 5.85 times a week on average. More than one in five say they make those checks more than ten times a week.

The findings point to a practical lesson for technology deployment: associates who participated in a pilot reported using most store tools at a rate of 74%, compared with 61% among those who were consulted before rollout and those who were never asked. Half of pilot participants reported high trust in their stock data, compared with 25% of those who were never asked for input.
